relaxations.why: An absent container and an empty one are different types in Rust: Option<Vec<T>> is not Vec<T>. There is no case where a caller has one and means the other, so a relaxation would widen nothing.

Rust's == already says NaN is unequal to itself, which is what the standard states by default. A caller wanting the other answer compares f64::to_bits or names the case, and a relaxation reaching inside a generic T: PartialEq is not expressible without a comparison routine this implementation does not have.

limits.what: Counts allocations exactly, once CountingAllocator is installed as the test binary's global allocator. Without it the assertion reports that nothing counted rather than passing.
limits.why: Rust counts every allocation through the allocator, as Go counts them through its runtime. What it cannot do is install a global allocator on a caller's behalf: a program has one, the program chooses it, and a library that took it would take it from the caller.

limits.what: Counts the calling thread's allocations exactly, once CountingAllocator is installed as the test binary's global allocator, so a test on another thread does not change the count. Without the allocator the assertion reports that nothing counted rather than passing.
limits.why: The allocator that counts for bench-max-allocs counts for this assertion too, and a library cannot install a global allocator on a caller's behalf.

limits.what: Counts bytes requested, once CountingAllocator is installed as the test binary's global allocator. Without it the assertion reports that nothing counted rather than passing.
limits.why: The same allocator answers both ceilings, so both stand or fall on it being installed. The count is of bytes asked for rather than bytes resident, which is what makes it stable across runs.

limits.what: Sees tasks spawned on the Tokio runtime the test is running under. A thread started with std::thread is not seen.
limits.why: Rust's standard library has no way to enumerate threads: nothing in std::thread lists them, so the synchronous crate cannot answer the question at all. Tokio counts its own live tasks, which is why this assertion ships in the tokio crate rather than the core.

surface.why: The seat states report and clock itself, with a default, so a seat that supplies neither gets the platform clock and a rendered sentence. Only a language whose interfaces carry no defaults needs a second interface to say the same thing.

The harness owns the loop here, so setup goes in a second closure, handed to measuring, that the harness runs outside the measurement. Marking the setup in place would need the body to reach the contract it was handed to, and two closures cannot hold one variable mutably, so the fixture would arrive through an Option that every benchmark unwraps.

equal takes two references of one type parameter, so a mismatched pair is already a compile error. A chain would hold a borrow of the subject across every method for no check the static form is missing.
